name: Nicoleño
confidence_why: one confirmed first-hand source; 4 other works read were silent
catalog_citation: Munro, Pamela. 2002. Takic foundations of Nicoleño vocabulary. In D. R. Browne, K. L. Mitchell & H. W. Chaney (eds.), Proceedings of the Fifth California Islands Symposium, 659-668. Santa Barbara: Santa Barbara Museum of Natural History (open PDF, sbbotanicgarden.org).
catalog_locator: pp. 666 (col. 2) - 667 (col. 1), discussion of Hardacre's stress marks, and p. 667 col. 1 summary paragraph (pdf pp. 8-9 of 10)
catalog_quote: Unlike Thompson and West’s, Hardacre’s words also indicate stress. In three of the forms, this is in the parenthesized pronunciation, which we have seen in almost every case to be less accurate than the spelling. In one case, however, stress is marked on the first version ... In ‘man’ and ‘sky’ stress is marked on exactly the same syllable as in all close cognates (those in which the second vowel of the proto-form is deleted), and if we interpret the marked accent on ‘body / wing’ as indicating first-syllable stress, that is probably expected too. ... The marked second-syllable stress in ‘hide’ (a stem with only short vowels in all languages) correlates exactly with the comparable Luiseño form, and this pattern is sufficiently rare, occurring within Cupan proper only in Luiseño and Juaneño (Munro 1990), that it most likely is also correct. Thus, the marked stresses probably date from the original recording rather than being added by a copyist. ... This short vocabulary reveals nothing about some phonological features of the language, such as vowel length, though it does suggest that stress in Nicoleño was an unpredictable lexical feature (as it is today in all Takic languages except Cahuilla) most like that seen in Luiseño and Juaneño.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: On the evidence of the four recorded words (náxe/náxi 'man', tóykwa 'sky', toká 'hide', pyúwke ~ púwke 'its wing'), stress is taken to be lexically specified and not predictable by position, patterning like Luiseño/Juaneño: first-syllable stress in three words, second-syllable stress in 'hide' matching the Luiseño cognate.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; Munro notes the stress marks come from Hardacre 1880 (three in the parenthesized pronunciations, one on the spelling) and argues they date from the original recording rather than a copyist; 'body/wing' stress placement is uncertain (piúuche or piuúche).
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms of four nouns only (one possessed noun); no phrase data; the whole claim is an inference from a four-word corpus plus Cupan comparison, explicitly hedged ('does suggest').
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog's 'Island Takic' (isla1277, no ISO code) is the language otherwise called Nicoleño, spoken on San Nicolas Island and known only from four words and two songs recorded from Juana María (the 'Lone Woman of San Nicolas Island', d. 1853). Munro 2002 is the sole linguistic analysis of the corpus; her stress remark is an inference from the accent marks in Hardacre's 1880 transcriptions of the four words compared with Cupan cognates, not a description of a spoken system.
